cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XXII
The slaughter in the hall.
But he stripped himself of his rags,\nOdysseus of the many designs,
and leapt to the great threshold with the bow and the\nquiver full of arrows, and poured out the swift shafts
there at his feet, and spoke among the suitors:
"So: that contest-past-all-contest is accomplished.
Now for another mark — one no man has ever hit —
and I shall know if I strike it:\nif Apollo gives me that glory."
He spoke, and leveled the bitter arrow at Antinous.
And he — he was that instant lifting a beautiful cup,\na golden one, two-eared, turning it in his hands
to drink the wine; and slaughter was not in his thoughts:
for who would think, among men at dinner, that one man\nin the middle of many — however strong he might be —
would bring on him foul death and the black doom?
But Odysseus took aim at his throat, and shot,\nand the point went clean on through the soft of the neck.
He sagged to one side; the cup dropped out of his\nhand as the arrow hit; and at once a thick jet came
up through his nostrils —\nhuman blood; and quick, with a kick,
he shoved the table from him and\nspilled the food to the floor:
the bread and the roast meats\nfouled in it. And the suitors
broke into uproar through the\nhouse when they saw the man fallen;
up from their chairs they started,\ndriven through the hall,
eyes darting every way along the well-built walls —
and nowhere was there a shield or a strong spear to seize.
And they raged at Odysseus with words of fury:
"Stranger, you shoot at men —\nand it will cost you! No more contests
for you: now your own sheer destruction is certain.
The man you have killed was the\nvery noblest of the young men
of Ithaca. For this the vultures will eat you — here."
So each man guessed: for indeed they thought he had killed
the man unwilling. The fools — they had not seen it yet:
that on every one of them the\ncords of death were fastened.
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"You dogs! You kept on saying\nI would never come home again
out of the land of Troy: and so you sheared away\nmy house, and lay with my slave-women by force,
and courted my own wife while I was still alive,\nfearing neither the gods who hold wide heaven
nor any vengeance of men, to come hereafter.
Now on you — on all of you —\nthe cords of death are fastened."
So he spoke; and the pale terror took hold of them all,
and every man peered round for a\nway to escape sheer destruction.
Only Eurymachus found words, and answered him:
"If you are truly Odysseus of Ithaca, come home again,
then all you say is just — all the Achaeans have done,
reckless things in plenty in the hall,\nin plenty on the land.
But there he lies — the man to blame for everything:
Antinous. He was the one who set these doings on —\nnot so much needing the marriage, or wanting it,
but with another purpose,\nwhich the son of Cronos never granted:
to be king himself in the land of well-built\nIthaca, and to ambush your son and kill him.
Now he is killed, as was his portion. You — spare your own
people; and we hereafter, making it good through the land,\nall that has been drunk and eaten in your halls,
each of us bringing a payment of twenty oxen's worth,\nwill pay you back in bronze and gold, until your heart
is warmed. Till then, no one could blame your anger."
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"Eurymachus — not if you handed over all your patrimonies,
everything you now have, and added more from elsewhere,
not even so would I hold my hands back from the killing\nbefore the suitors had paid for the whole trespass.
Now the choice lies before you: fight me face to face,\nor run — whoever can slip his death and doom.
But I do not think one man of\nyou escapes sheer destruction."
And their knees went slack where\nthey stood, and their hearts.
And Eurymachus called out among them a second time:
"Friends — this man will not\nnow hold his invincible hands.
He has the polished bow and the quiver: he will shoot\nfrom the smooth threshold until he has killed us all.
Then let our minds be on battle! Draw your swords,\nput up the tables against the arrows of quick death,
and let us all go at him in one body — see if we can\nshove him off the threshold and out of the doors,
then through the town, and the alarm raised at once!
Then this man would soon have shot his last."
So speaking, he drew his sharp sword,\nbronze, two-edged, and leapt at him
with a blood-freezing yell.\nBut in the same instant noble Odysseus
let the arrow fly, and struck his chest beside the nipple,
and drove the swift shaft into his liver. Out of his hand
the sword dropped to the ground; he doubled over the table
and crumpled, sprawling across it,\nand spilled the food to the floor
and the two-eared cup. His forehead beat the\nearth in his heart's agony; both feet kicked out,
rattling the chair; and the\nmist poured down over his eyes.
Then Amphinomus went for glorious Odysseus,\ncharging him head-on, his sharp sword drawn,
to see if he might give way from the doors. But Telemachus
was too quick: he caught him\nfrom behind with the bronze spear
square between the shoulders,\nand drove it through his chest,
and he fell with a crash, and struck\nthe ground full with his forehead.
And Telemachus sprang back,\nleaving the long-shadowed spear
there in Amphinomus: for he feared that as he pulled\nthe long spear out, some Achaean might rush in
and cut him with a sword, or strike him as he stooped.
He ran, and came quickly to his dear father,\nand standing close he spoke winged words:
"Father — now I will bring you a shield and two spears\nand a helmet all of bronze, fitted to your temples;
and I will arm myself as I go, and give the swineherd\nthe same, and the cowherd. Armored is better."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Run — bring them, while I\nstill have arrows to fight with,
or they will force me from the doors, one man alone."
So he spoke; and Telemachus obeyed his dear father
and went to the storeroom where\nthe famous arms were lying.
He took out four shields, and eight spears,\nand four bronze helmets thick with horsehair,
and came carrying them fast to his dear father.
He girded the bronze on his own body first,\nand in the same way the two slaves put on the fine armor,
and they took their stand around Odysseus —\nthe deep mind, the shifting counsels.
And he, so long as he had arrows to fight with,\nkept aiming, and dropping suitors in his own house,
one man after another: they fell in heaps.
But when the arrows failed the master archer,
he leaned the bow against the\ndoorpost of the strong-built hall,
to stand there by the shining entrance-wall,\nand threw about his shoulders a shield of four hides,
and set on his mighty head a well-made helmet,\nhorsehair-crested, the plume nodding terror from the top,
and took up two strong spears, headed with bronze.
Now there was a raised side-door in the well-built wall,
and level with the top of the threshold of the strong hall
an exit to a passage, closed with well-fitted boards.
Odysseus set the noble swineherd to watch it,\nposted close: it was the single way out.
And Agelaus spoke to them all,\nputting the word to everyone:
"Friends — could not someone climb through the side-door
and get word to the people,\nand the alarm be raised at once?
Then this man would soon have shot his last."
Then Melanthius the goatherd answered him:
"No way, Agelaus, Zeus-nurtured:\nthe fine gates of the courtyard
are terribly near, and the mouth of the passage is cruel:
one man could hold it against all comers —\nany man with strength in him.
No — wait: let me bring you armor from the storeroom
to harness you. For it is in there,\nI am certain — nowhere else —
that Odysseus and his shining son have stowed the arms."
So speaking, Melanthius the goatherd climbed up
through the smoke-vents of the\nhall to the storerooms of Odysseus,
and took out twelve shields, as many spears,\nas many bronze helmets thick with horsehair,
and came back fast and gave them to the suitors.
And then the knees of Odysseus went slack, and his heart,
when he saw them buckling on the armor and brandishing
the long spears in their hands:\nthe work now looked great to him.
And quickly he spoke winged words to Telemachus:
"Telemachus — one of the women in the halls is stoking\nthe evil war against us — that, or it is Melanthius."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Father, the fault is mine — my own, no other's —\nI left the storeroom's close-fitted door
standing ajar. Their lookout was sharper than I was.
Go, noble Eumaeus: close the storeroom door,\nand find out whether it is one of the women doing this,
or Dolius' son Melanthius — he is the one I think it is."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And Melanthius the goatherd went again to the storeroom
to bring out more fine armor.\nBut the noble swineherd marked him,
and quickly said to Odysseus, standing near:
"Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —
there he goes again, that ruinous man, the one we guessed:
into the storeroom. Tell me straight out:
do I kill him — if I prove the better man —\nor bring him here to you, to pay for the trespasses,
the many, that man has schemed in your house?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"I and Telemachus will hold the lordly suitors\npenned inside the hall, rage as they may.
You two: twist his feet and hands behind him,\nthrow him into the storeroom, tie boards fast at his back,
make a braided rope fast to him, and haul him\nup the tall pillar, up close to the roof-beams —
so that he lives on a long while, suffering hard pains."
So he spoke; and they listened well and obeyed:
they went to the storeroom —\nthe man inside did not see them —
and there he was, hunting armor in the room's far corner,
while the two of them stood waiting\neither side of the doorposts.
And as Melanthius the goatherd came over the threshold,\nin one hand carrying a beautiful helmet,
in the other a broad shield,\nan old one, mottled with mildew —
the hero Laertes' shield,\nwhich he carried in his young days,
long since laid by,\nthe stitches of its straps rotted out —
the two of them sprang and seized him,\nand dragged him in by the hair,
and threw him to the floor for all his anguish of heart,
and bound his feet and hands with a heart-grieving knot,
wrenched hard behind him, through and through,\nas ordered by Laertes' son, much-enduring noble Odysseus;
then they made a braided rope fast to him, and hauled\nhim up the tall pillar, up close to the roof-beams.
And taunting him you spoke, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Now you will keep watch indeed,\nMelanthius — the whole night through,
stretched out on the sort of soft bed you deserve;\nand the early-born one out of Ocean's streams will not
slip past you as she comes,\non her golden throne, at the hour
you drive in goats for the suitors,\nto make their feast in the hall."
So he was left there, racked in the deadly binding;\nand the two got into their armor, shut the shining door,
and went back to Odysseus —\nthe deep mind, the shifting counsels.
There they stood, breathing fury: on the threshold\nfour men; inside the hall, many men, and good ones.
And now Athena, daughter of Zeus, came near them,\nlikened to Mentor in body and in voice.
Odysseus was glad at the sight of her, and said:
"Mentor — beat off ruin! Remember your old companion,\nwho did you good service — and you my own age-mate!"
So he spoke, guessing it was Athena, rouser of armies.
And the suitors on their side bellowed through the hall,\nAgelaus, Damastor's son, first to threaten her:
"Mentor — don't let Odysseus talk you around\ninto fighting the suitors and defending him.
For here is how I think our purpose will be accomplished:
when we have killed these two, father and son,\nyou will be killed with them — for the things you are minded
to do in this hall. Your own head will pay the price.
And when the bronze has stripped the force from\nall of you, everything you own, indoors and out,
we will pool with the goods of Odysseus. Your sons\nwe will not let live in your halls; your daughters
and your true-hearted wife will not\nwalk free in the town of Ithaca."
So he spoke; and Athena's heart grew angrier yet,\nand she lashed Odysseus with words of fury:
"Odysseus — where is your strength gone?\nWhere is the fight in you —
you who for Helen's sake,\nthe white-armed, the nobly fathered,
nine years on end battled the Trojans without a\nbreak and killed many men in the terrible fighting?
By your counsel the wide-wayed city of Priam was taken!
How is it that now, come home to your own house and goods,
face to face with the suitors,\nyou whimper about being brave?
Here, old friend — stand by me and watch the work,\nand learn what kind of man, among enemy fighters,
Mentor, Alcimus' son, is at repaying kindness."
She spoke — and did not yet grant\nvictory outright to either side,
but went on testing the strength and\nfight of Odysseus and of his glorious son.
And she herself darted up to the\nroof-beam of the smoke-stained hall
and perched there — like a swallow, face-on.
Now Agelaus, Damastor's son, rallied the suitors,\nwith Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus,
Peisander Polyctor's son, and Polybus the shrewd:
for these were far the best of the suitors in prowess,\nof all who still lived and fought for their lives —
the rest the bow and the crowding arrows had brought down.
And Agelaus spoke to them all,\nputting the word to everyone:
"Friends — now this man's invincible hands will stop.
Mentor has left him — after the empty boasting —\nand they are alone at the outer doors.
So do not throw your long spears all together:
come — you six throw first, and see if Zeus will\ngrant that Odysseus be hit, and we win the glory.
The rest are no concern, once that man falls."
So he spoke; and they all threw as he ordered,\nhungry for it. And Athena made every cast come to nothing:
one man's spear struck the doorpost of the strong-built hall,\nanother's the close-fitted door itself,
another's ash shaft, heavy with\nbronze, slammed into the wall.
And when they had weathered the suitors' spears,\nmuch-enduring noble Odysseus began among his men:
"Friends — now it is mine to say it: throw!
Into the crowd of the suitors — men wild to strip\nour corpses on top of the wrongs they did before."
So he spoke; and they all threw their sharp spears,\naiming straight ahead: Odysseus killed Demoptolemus;
Telemachus, Euryades; the swineherd, Elatus;\nand the man in charge of the cattle killed Peisander.
All of those together bit the vast floor with their teeth,
and the suitors fell back into the deep of the hall;
and the others charged,\nand pulled their spears from the corpses.
Again the suitors threw their sharp spears, hungry for it;\nand Athena made the many casts come to nothing:
one man's spear struck the doorpost of the strong-built hall,\nanother's the close-fitted door itself,
another's ash shaft, heavy with\nbronze, slammed into the wall.
But Amphimedon caught Telemachus on the wrist —\na graze: the bronze just broke the surface of the skin;
and Ctesippus, over the shield, scratched Eumaeus
on the shoulder with his long spear:\nit skipped and fell to earth.
Then those around Odysseus —\nthe deep mind, the shifting counsels —
threw their sharp spears into the crowd of the suitors:
and this time Eurydamas fell\nto Odysseus, sacker of cities;
Amphimedon to Telemachus; Polybus to the swineherd;
and then Ctesippus fell to the\nman in charge of the cattle,
struck full in the chest; and he crowed over him:
"Son of Polytherses — you lover\nof a good jeer! — never again
give way to your folly and talk big. Leave the\nword to the gods: they are far stronger than you.
This is your guest-gift in return — to match the ox-hoof
you gave godlike Odysseus once,\nwhen he begged through his own hall."
So spoke the herdsman of the\nspiral-horned cattle. And Odysseus
wounded Damastor's son, close in, with the long spear;\nand Telemachus wounded Leocritus, Evenor's son,
clean in the flank with his spear,\nand drove the bronze through:
he pitched forward and struck the\nground full with his forehead.
And now Athena raised the aegis that wastes mankind,\nhigh from the roof; and their wits scattered in terror,
and they stampeded through the hall like a herd of cattle
when the darting gadfly falls on them and whirls them wild
in the season of spring, when the long days come in.
And the others — like vultures\nwith hooked claws and curving beaks
that come down out of the mountains on the smaller birds:
these skim the plain, cowering away from the clouds,\nbut the vultures stoop and kill them; no defense,
no flight — and men delight to watch the hunting:
so those four, rushing the suitors through the house,
struck them down left and right; and hideous groaning rose
as heads were smashed, and the\nwhole floor smoked with blood.
But Leodes ran in and caught Odysseus by the knees,\nand clasping them in supplication spoke winged words:
"By your knees, Odysseus — respect me, pity me!
I tell you I never said a word to any woman in your halls,\nnever did one reckless thing — no: I kept trying
to stop the others, the suitors,\nwhen one would do such things.
But they would not listen,\nwould not hold their hands from evil,
and so through their own recklessness\nthey have met an ugly fate.
And I, their sacrifice-diviner, having done nothing,
am to lie down with them: no thanks,\nhereafter, for good service!"
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"If you declare yourself their sacrifice-diviner,
then many a time, no doubt,\nyou must have prayed in my halls
that the accomplishment of my\nsweet homecoming be far away —
that my dear wife go with you, and bear you children.
For that you shall not slip\nbeneath a death that lays men low."
So speaking, he took up in his strong hand a sword\nthat lay there — Agelaus had dropped it to the ground
as he was killed — and drove it\nthrough the middle of his neck:
and while he was still speaking,\nhis head mixed with the dust.
But the singer still dodged the black doom — Terpes' son,
Phemius, who sang among the suitors under compulsion.
He stood with the clear lyre in his hands close\nby the side-door, and his mind was split two ways:
whether to slip out of the hall to the great altar of Zeus
of the Courtyard, and sit there on the masoned\nstone where Laertes and Odysseus had burned so many
thighbones of oxen — or rush\nforward and clasp Odysseus' knees.
And as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better way:
to take hold of the knees of Laertes' son Odysseus.
So he set the hollow lyre down on the ground between\nthe mixing-bowl and the silver-studded chair,
and rushed forward himself and\ncaught Odysseus by the knees,
and clasping them in supplication spoke winged words:
"By your knees, Odysseus — respect me, pity me!
On you yourself the grief will fall hereafter,\nif you kill a singer — me — who sing for gods and for men.
I am self-taught: a god has planted in my heart all\nthe pathways of song; and I am fit to sing beside you
as beside a god. Do not be hungry to cut my throat.
And Telemachus would tell you this — your own dear son:
that it was never by my will, never for want of mine,
that I came to your house to sing at the suitors' feasts:
they were more, and stronger —\nthey marched me here by force."
And the sacred strength of Telemachus heard him,\nand quickly spoke to his father, standing near:
"Stop! He is guiltless — do not cut him with the bronze.
And Medon the herald let us save as well,\nwho always cared for me in our house when I was a child —
unless Philoetius has killed him already, or the swineherd,\nor he met you as you stormed along the hall."
So he spoke; and Medon heard him — a man of sensible\nmind — for he lay cowering under a chair, wrapped up
in a fresh-flayed oxhide, dodging the black doom.
Up from under the chair he came\nat once, stripped off the oxhide,
and rushed forward and caught Telemachus by the knees,\nand clasping them in supplication spoke winged words:
"Friend — here I am: myself!\nHold back, and tell your father,
before in his overmastering strength\nhe cuts me down with the sharp bronze
in his rage at the suitor-men — the men who sheared away
his goods in the halls,\nand honored you not at all, the fools."
And Odysseus of the many designs smiled at him and said:
"Take heart: this man has pulled you clear and saved you —
so you may know in your heart, and tell another too,\nhow doing good outruns doing evil, and by far.
Now out of the hall with you, and sit in the courtyard,
away from the slaughter —\nyou and the singer of many songs —
while I finish in the house the work that I must."
So he spoke; and the two of them went out of the\nhall and sat down by the altar of great Zeus,
peering about on every side, expecting death each moment.
And Odysseus peered through his own house, for any man\nstill living, hiding there, dodging the black doom.
But he saw them all, the whole count of them,\nin blood and dust fallen — so many, like fish that fishermen
have hauled from the gray sea in the mesh of a net\nonto the curved beach: heaped on the sand they lie,
all of them, aching for the waves of the sea,\nand the shining Sun takes the life out of them:
so the suitors lay heaped on one another.
Then Odysseus of the many designs said to Telemachus:
"Telemachus — go, call me the nurse Eurycleia,\nso I can tell her the word that is on my mind."
So he spoke; and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,\nand rattling the door he called the nurse Eurycleia:
"Up with you, and come, old woman born long ago —\nyou who are overseer of our serving-women in the halls.
Come: my father calls you; he has something to say."
So he spoke; and for her the word stayed wingless.
She opened the doors of the well-settled halls\nand came; and Telemachus led the way before her.
And she found Odysseus among the bodies of the slain,\nspattered with blood and gore, like a lion
that comes from feeding on an ox of the farmstead:
all his chest, and his cheeks on either side,\nare bloody, and he is terrible to look in the face:
so was Odysseus spattered — feet, and hands above them.
And she — when she saw the corpses and the sea of blood,
she opened her mouth to raise\nthe cry of triumph: such a work
she saw accomplished. But Odysseus\nchecked her, and held her back,
hot as she was, and spoke winged words to her:
"In your own heart rejoice,\nold woman — and hold it in: no cries.
It is unholy to glory over slaughtered men.
These men the doom of the gods has broken,\nand their own ruthless deeds:
for they honored nobody on this earth,\nbad man or good, whoever came among them —
and so through their own recklessness\nthey have met an ugly fate.
But come now, name me the women of the halls:
which of them dishonor me, and which are guiltless."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered him:
"Then I will tell you, child, the whole truth of it.
You have fifty serving-women in your halls —\nslave-women we have taught to work their work,
to card the wool and to bear the lot of slavery.
Of these, twelve in all have\nwalked the road of shamelessness:
no respect for me — none for Penelope herself.
Telemachus is only newly grown; his mother would\nnot let him give commands to the serving-women.
But come — let me climb to the bright upper room and\ntell your wife. Some god has laid a sleep on her."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Do not wake her yet. Tell them to come here —\nthe women who all this while contrived their shamelessness."
So he spoke; and the old woman went off down the\nhall to carry word to the women and hurry them along.
And he called Telemachus to his side, and the cowherd,\nand the swineherd, and spoke winged words to them:
"Begin carrying out the dead, and set the women to it;\nand after that, the beautiful chairs and the tables —
have them cleaned with water and porous sponges.
And when you have set the whole house in order,\nlead the serving-women out of the strong-built hall
to the spot between the roundhouse\nand the good courtyard fence,
and cut them down with the long\nswords, till you have stripped
the life from all of them,\nand they have forgotten Aphrodite —
the sweetness they took under\nthe suitors, coupling in secret."
So he spoke; and the women came in a huddle, all of them,\nwailing terribly, the big tears streaming down.
First they carried out the corpses of the dead and laid\nthem under the portico of the well-fenced courtyard,
propping them against each other; and Odysseus commanded,
hurrying the work himself;\nand they carried them out — under force.
And after that they cleaned the beautiful chairs\nand the tables with water and porous sponges;
and Telemachus, with the cowherd and the swineherd,\nscraped the floor of the strong-founded house
with hoes, and the slave-women\ncarried the scrapings out of doors.
And when they had set the whole hall in order,\nthey led the serving-women out of the strong-built hall
to the spot between the roundhouse\nand the good courtyard fence,
and penned them in the narrow place,\nwhere there was no way out.
And clear-headed Telemachus began, and spoke among them:
"By no clean death will I take the lives of these —\nthese who poured their insults on my head,
on my own mother, and slept beside the suitors."
So he spoke; and he made the cable of a dark-prowed ship
fast to a great pillar, and flung it round the roundhouse,
stretched taut, up high,\nso no foot could reach the ground.
And as when thrushes with their long wings,\nor doves, strike into a snare set up in a thicket,
heading in to roost, and a hateful bed receives them:
so the women held their heads in a row, and round every
neck a noose was laid, that they might die most pitiably.
They kicked out with their feet\na little while — not very long.
And Melanthius they dragged out\nthrough the porch and the courtyard:
they sliced away his nose and\nears with the pitiless bronze
and tore out his genitals, raw meat for the dogs to share,
and lopped off his hands and feet in their fury of heart.
Then they washed their own hands and feet and went\ninto the house to Odysseus: the work was accomplished.
And he spoke to the dear nurse Eurycleia:
"Bring sulfur, old woman —\nthe cure of evils — and bring me fire,
so I can fume the hall with it. And bid Penelope\ncome down to me, with her attendant women;
and rouse all the serving-women in the house to come."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered him:
"Yes, my child — all this you have said as it should be.
But come, let me bring you clothes, a cloak and a tunic:
do not stand in your halls like this,\nwith your broad shoulders
wrapped in rags. That would be a thing to blame."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"First of all: let there be fire for me in the hall."
So he spoke; and the dear nurse Eurycleia did not disobey,\nbut brought the fire and the sulfur; and Odysseus
fumed through and through the hall,\nthe house, the courtyard.
And the old woman went off up through\nthe beautiful house of Odysseus
to carry word to the women and hurry them along;\nand out of the hall they came, torches in their hands,
and they poured around Odysseus, and embraced him,\nand kissed his head and his shoulders, welcoming him,
catching and clasping his hands;\nand a sweet longing seized him
to weep and to sob: for in his heart he knew them all.
